newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt scooping up wheat with new vigour.
newsitem.headline: Egypt scooping up wheat with new vigour.

text.p: Egypt's unpredictable official commodities buyer took advantage of a temporary freeze of a controversial decree on genetically altered crops and re-entered the grain market with a vengeance on Tuesday, traders said.

Samir el-Shakankiri, the country's major buyer, had tendered late on Monday for 50,000 tonnes of U.S. or French wheat but ended up on Tuesday buying 450,000 tonnes of American soft red wheat for August delivery at prices of $127 and $127.40.
He said earlier on Tuesday he was seeking an additional 50,000 tonnes of French wheat, although European traders said the cost per tonne was less competitive than the lower American prices.

Traders in Cairo said they were not surprised at Shakankiri's decision to buy so much wheat because of the unclear status of a controversial health ministry decree requiring proof that grain imports had not been genetically altered.
Late on Monday, Shakankiri told Reuters he had received a permit allowing him to buy "for the time being" wheat which did not have a certificate that it had not been genetically engineered.
He had said earlier the same day he would not enter the market for up to a month, or until issues raised by the decree were sorted out.
European traders said Egypt normally bought about 400,000 tonnes of wheat a month and needed to buy wheat to cover its needs for August onwards.
"Shakankiri wants to buy as much as he can as soon as he can and take advantage of the situation," a Cairo trader said.
The traders also said the mercurial Shakankiri usually used his tenders for small quantities as bait, and had in the past bought much more than he was initially seeking.
"It's just his nature... that's the way he plays the market, he likes to feel it out," another trader said.

The health ministry decree, dated July 1 but made available only last week, has stymied traders whose grain shipments -- in the ports or on the high seas -- are being held ransom until further clarification.
The decree does not say when it comes into effect or where traders can get the required certificates.

On Tuesday, traders said they thought the decree had been amended and based their assumptions on a memorandum from a junior health ministry official, obtained by Reuters, requesting the health minister to delay implementing it until October and asking him to let in all grain shipments, except for "suspect soybeans".

Although there is no genetically engineered wheat on the market, corn and soybean crops have been genetically altered. Egypt imports about 6.5 million tonnes of wheat a year as well as hundreds of thousands of tonnes of corn and soybean.
"No one knows for sure whether this memorandum has been approved, we're just hearing talk from traders who can't afford not to act on the assumption that it has been," a trader said.
"As far as we know this is how it will work for now. The whole decree business was stupid and now they're just burying their heads in the sand until October," he added.

An official at the U.S. embassy, whose country is a major grain exporter to Egypt and an advocate of genetic engineering, said the U.S. Department of Agriculture was trying to get Egypt to scrap the decree totally because the problem would resurface again after three months.
"And three months is not all that long a time. It won't get many shipments delivered," he added.
